units: Von Neumann architecture, the control unit and ALU, registers and the fetch–decode–execute cycle

The Central Processing Unit (CPU) processes instructions from programs. It fetches instructions from main memory, decodes them and executes operations. It performs a very large number of simple operations each second.
In Von Neumann architecture, program instructions and the data used by those programs are stored in the same main memory. The CPU fetches both from RAM. This is the stored-program principle.
The control unit coordinates CPU activities, interprets instructions and issues control signals. It organises the timing and sequence of work with the system clock.
The ALU carries out arithmetic such as addition and subtraction, and logical operations such as AND, OR and NOT. The result of a calculation can be held temporarily in the accumulator.
Registers are very small, exceptionally fast storage locations inside the CPU. Cache is also fast memory near or on the processor, but is normally slower than registers and faster than RAM.

The Program Counter holds the memory address of the next instruction to fetch. For a simple sequential program it increases as each instruction is fetched. A branch instruction can change the next address.
The Memory Address Register holds the address of the memory location being accessed, whether that location contains an instruction or data. It identifies WHERE the CPU needs to look.
The Memory Data Register temporarily holds an instruction or data being transferred to or from main memory. It holds WHAT has been fetched or is being written.
The accumulator temporarily holds the result of arithmetic or logical work. For example, an ADD instruction can use the ALU to calculate a value and place the result in the ACC.

Fetch: use the PC and MAR to find an instruction in RAM and bring it into the MDR. Decode: the CU interprets the instruction. Execute: perform the operation, sometimes fetching data or storing a result. Repeat for the next instruction.

An instruction such as ADD #6 adds the constant 6 directly. An instruction such as ADD 30 fetches the value held at memory address 30. The address and the value stored at that address are different things.
Clock speed, processing cores and cache size, including comparisons between processors
The three factors emphasised in this unit are clock speed, number of CPU cores and cache size. They can improve performance, but the software and task also matter.

Clock speed measures clock cycles per second, in hertz (Hz). 1 GHz means one billion clock cycles per second. Raising clock speed can help a processor complete work faster, but clock cycles do not always correspond to one completed instruction.
A dual-core CPU has two processing cores; a quad-core CPU has four. Multiple cores can work on separate tasks or parts of one suitably designed task at the same time.
Why more cores are not always faster

Some workloads cannot be split effectively between cores. A program that mainly uses one core may see little speed increase from extra cores. Core count alone is not a reliable measure of overall performance.
Cache stores frequently or recently used instructions and data so the processor does not need to access slower RAM as often. A cache hit is generally faster than a cache miss.
L1 cache is usually the smallest and fastest, close to a core. L2 is typically larger and a little slower. L3 is usually larger again and often shared by multiple cores. Exact sizes vary by CPU.
To evaluate CPU performance, consider clock speed, cores, cache and the kinds of programs being run together. Avoid assuming that doubling clock speed or cores always doubles real-world performance.

A strong explanation links a feature to its effect: more cache can reduce slow RAM accesses; additional cores can handle parallel tasks; higher clock frequency allows more processing cycles per second, within other constraints.
Dedicated computer systems inside larger devices, their inputs, outputs and reliability
An embedded system is a computer system built into a larger device to perform one or a small set of specialised control tasks. It commonly uses sensors or other inputs, processing and outputs.

An embedded system is usually designed for a specific purpose; a general-purpose computer is designed to run many different applications. An embedded system may still be updated, but its tasks are more restricted.
For example, a dishwasher senses temperature and water level (input), checks the selected cycle (processing), then controls a heater or pump (output). This is input–process–output in action.
Embedded systems include microwave controllers, washing machine control units, burglar alarms, digital watches, satnav units and vehicle engine control and safety systems.
Examples include cruise control, cooling fans, air conditioning, parking cameras, interior lighting and engine management. Each uses information to control a specialised function.

An embedded controller may be expected to operate reliably without constant user intervention. When a controller handles heating, braking or safety, incorrect behaviour can have important consequences.
RAM, ROM, volatile and non-volatile memory, loading applications and virtual memory
In the stored-program model, the CPU needs fast access to instructions and data belonging to running programs. Main memory stores this working information while programs execute.
RAM stores the currently used operating-system components, applications and data they are working on. It can be read from and written to. RAM loses its contents when the power is removed.
Volatile storage loses stored data without power, like RAM. Non-volatile storage retains data, like ROM, SSDs and hard disks. This distinction matters when saving work.

ROM is non-volatile memory used for essential start-up instructions and firmware. In the unit materials, ROM includes the bootstrap and BIOS. It is not used as working memory for ordinary applications.
Firmware starts the computer, initialises hardware and starts the process of loading an operating system. The bootstrap instructions help locate and load the operating system from secondary storage.

Files and installed software remain on secondary storage when the computer is switched off. When software runs, the required instructions and data are loaded into RAM so the CPU can access them quickly.

When there is not enough available RAM, the operating system can use part of secondary storage as virtual memory. Data is moved between RAM and the storage device, allowing memory demand to be managed.

An SSD or HDD is slower than RAM. Frequent swapping of data between RAM and the storage device can noticeably reduce performance. Virtual memory is not a like-for-like replacement for enough physical RAM.

In general, CPU registers are fastest but tiny; cache is fast and small; RAM is larger and slower than cache; secondary storage is much larger but slower. Different types balance speed, capacity and cost.
Magnetic, optical and solid-state technologies, storage characteristics and capacity calculations
Secondary storage keeps operating systems, applications and user files when power is off. It is non-volatile and generally offers much more capacity than primary memory.
A hard disk drive (HDD) stores information magnetically on spinning platters. Read/write heads move to access tracks and sectors. Magnetic tape is also used for some backup and archival work.
HDDs can offer large capacities at relatively low cost per gigabyte. Moving parts can make them less durable when dropped and access can be slower than on SSDs.
CDs, DVDs and Blu-ray discs use a laser to read the surface. Pits and lands affect reflected light. Optical media is portable, but generally slower and has less capacity than common HDDs or SSDs.
The lesson examples include CDs around 700 MB, DVDs up to about 8.4 GB for a dual-layer disc and dual-layer Blu-ray discs around 50 GB. The technologies pack data at different densities.
SSDs, USB flash drives and SD cards use non-volatile electronic memory. They have no mechanical read/write heads or spinning platters, making them fast and resistant to some physical impacts.

Magnetic: often cost-effective for large capacities. Optical: removable discs suitable for certain distribution or archival uses. Solid-state: fast, compact and often highly portable, but can cost more per gigabyte.

Capacity is how much fits. Speed is how fast data is read/written. Portability is ease of carrying. Durability is resistance to damage. Reliability is likelihood of preserving data. Cost includes price and cost per unit stored.
Choose storage by explaining WHY its characteristics suit the use: an SSD for a laptop that is carried around; a large HDD for economical bulk storage; an SD card for a compatible camera.
Total size = number of files × average file size. For example, 2,400 photos at 5 MB each need 12,000 MB, approximately 12 GB using the unit's decimal convention of 1 GB = 1,000 MB.
A device with more capacity does not automatically transfer data faster. A storage recommendation should consider speed, cost, durability and portability as well as capacity.

flash.a: Not every task can use all four cores in parallel.

flash.q: Where is cache relative to RAM in the speed hierarchy?

flash.q: Give a car example of an embedded controller.
flash.a: Engine control, cruise control or cooling fan control.

flash.q: Is a laptop usually an embedded system?

flash.a: It is lost because RAM is volatile.

quiz.q: A processor fetches an instruction at address 42. Which register should hold 42 while accessing RAM?
quiz.why: The MAR holds the memory address being accessed.

quiz.q: After fetching a sequential instruction, which register normally points ahead?
quiz.why: The Program Counter identifies the next instruction to fetch.

quiz.q: Which item temporarily contains a fetched instruction?
quiz.why: The MDR holds the actual data or instruction transferred.

quiz.q: A processor performs a subtraction. Which component carries out the arithmetic?
quiz.why: The ALU performs arithmetic and logical work.

quiz.q: What does the Control Unit mainly do?
quiz.why: The CU organises and controls processor operations.

quiz.q: A program adds a constant directly to the accumulator. Which notation indicates an immediate value?
quiz.why: The # in the teaching model indicates a literal constant.

quiz.q: What does stored-program architecture keep together in memory?
options: Only compiled programs and no data
quiz.why: Von Neumann systems store program instructions and data in main memory.

quiz.q: Which memory location holds an ALU result temporarily?
quiz.why: The accumulator is used for intermediate results.

quiz.q: Which description of a CPU register is most accurate?
options: Tiny, very fast storage within the processor
quiz.why: Registers provide fast temporary storage inside the CPU.

quiz.q: Which sequence best describes the repeated instruction cycle?
quiz.why: The CPU repeatedly fetches, decodes and executes instructions.

quiz.q: A CPU wants the data at address 71. What is the difference between MAR and MDR?
options: MDR holds 71; MAR performs the calculation
Both always store the same address
MAR holds 71; MDR holds the fetched value
quiz.why: MAR is an address register, MDR a data register.

quiz.q: A processor runs at 2.5 GHz. What quantity does this describe?
quiz.why: GHz measures clock frequency, not storage capacity.

quiz.q: Which change can improve a highly parallel workload?
quiz.why: Parallel tasks can make productive use of additional cores.

quiz.q: Why might a single-threaded program see little benefit from eight cores?
options: All cores are slower than RAM
It cannot effectively use many cores at once
The screen refresh rate is fixed
quiz.why: An unsplit workload may run largely on one core.

quiz.q: Which of these is normally fastest to access?
quiz.why: L1 cache is closest to the core and usually the fastest cache level.

quiz.q: What is a cache hit?
options: Data is written to optical media
Requested data is found in cache
quiz.why: Cache hits avoid a slower fetch from main memory.

quiz.q: What might a larger useful cache reduce?
options: The value of the program counter
quiz.why: Cache can retain frequently needed data or instructions.

quiz.q: Which cache level is often shared by several cores?
quiz.why: L3 cache is commonly shared among cores.

quiz.q: Two CPUs have the same clock speed. What else can change performance?
quiz.why: The slides highlight cores and cache as further factors.

quiz.q: Does twice the clock frequency guarantee twice the real-world speed?
options: Only for files larger than a GB
No, other architecture and workload limits matter
quiz.why: Clock frequency contributes to performance but is not the only factor.

quiz.q: Which workload is more likely to benefit from multiple cores?
options: A single serial operation with no parallel work
quiz.why: Independent work can be distributed to separate cores.

quiz.q: Which device most clearly contains a dedicated embedded controller?
quiz.why: A washing machine has a controller for specific tasks.

quiz.q: What is the main purpose of an embedded computer?
options: Control a specific function within a larger device
quiz.why: Embedded computers specialise in defined control tasks.

quiz.q: In a smart thermostat, which is an input?
options: A printout of the final result
quiz.why: Temperature sensors provide measurements as inputs.

quiz.q: In a burglar alarm, which is an output?
quiz.why: A siren is an output controlled by the system.

quiz.q: Which vehicle component commonly uses embedded control?
quiz.why: Engine control units manage specialised engine functions.

quiz.q: Why is reliability particularly important in a safety controller?
options: It must render every video format
Incorrect behaviour may affect physical safety
quiz.why: Controllers used for safety-critical tasks need dependable behaviour.

quiz.q: Which best describes general-purpose software support?
options: Only one fixed function is ever possible
Many different applications can be installed and run
It cannot connect to a keyboard
quiz.why: A general-purpose computer is designed for varied user tasks.

quiz.q: What is an example of processing in an embedded device?
options: Comparing a sensor reading against a threshold
quiz.why: Processing applies rules to the input before selecting an output.

quiz.q: What kind of memory normally holds an active web browser and its working data?
quiz.why: RAM stores currently running applications and their working data.

quiz.q: Which characteristic means information disappears when power is lost?
quiz.why: RAM is volatile.

quiz.q: Which memory is intended to retain basic start-up firmware without power?
quiz.why: ROM is non-volatile and stores essential start-up instructions in the taught model.

quiz.q: What does RAM stand for?
quiz.why: RAM means Random Access Memory.

quiz.q: Why are programs loaded from secondary storage into RAM?
options: RAM is always larger than the SSD
The CPU needs fast working access
HDDs can no longer store programs
quiz.why: RAM is faster for working instructions and data.

quiz.q: What can happen when running programs need more RAM than is available?
options: The system may use secondary storage as virtual memory
The CPU no longer runs instructions
quiz.why: Virtual memory can move some working data onto secondary storage.

quiz.q: What is a common drawback of heavy virtual-memory use?
options: Slow performance caused by data transfers
Permanent storage of all unsaved edits
quiz.why: Secondary storage is slower to access than RAM.

quiz.q: Which retains data after shutting down normally?
quiz.why: SSDs are non-volatile.

quiz.q: Which component temporarily holds an application's actively used document?
options: A laser in an optical drive
quiz.why: Active data is normally held in RAM.

quiz.q: Which sequence best describes starting an installed application?
options: Load from the monitor into ROM
Load program data from SSD/HDD into RAM, then CPU executes instructions
Write all data to the keyboard
Send the program to the cooling fan
quiz.why: Secondary storage holds installed software and RAM provides working memory.

quiz.q: Which device uses rotating magnetic platters?
quiz.why: HDDs use magnetic platters and read/write heads.

quiz.q: Which device generally has no moving storage mechanism?
quiz.why: Solid-state storage uses electronic memory cells.

quiz.q: How does an optical drive read a disc?
options: By scanning a printed QR code
quiz.why: Optical discs have surface features read using light.

quiz.q: A photographer wants removable storage for a compatible camera. What fits best?
quiz.why: An SD card is small, portable, and non-volatile.

quiz.q: A club needs economical bulk storage for many video archives. Which choice is typically suitable?
quiz.why: HDDs offer large capacities at a relatively low cost.

quiz.q: Which matters most if a drive must survive frequent carrying and bumps?
quiz.why: Durability describes resistance to physical damage.

quiz.q: Which describes storage reliability?
options: The number of USB ports on the case
How likely data is to remain available without being lost
quiz.why: Reliability concerns preserving data.

quiz.q: Which device uses the storage method magnetic?
quiz.why: Magnetic tape records information magnetically.

quiz.q: Which storage characteristic describes reading 250 MB per second?
quiz.why: A transfer rate describes speed.

quiz.q: A music collection has 850 files averaging 4 MB. Approximately how much space is needed?
quiz.why: 850 × 4 = 3,400 MB = about 3.4 GB in decimal units.

quiz.q: About how many 25 MB videos fit in 5 GB of available space, using decimal units?
Which comparison is generally sound?
options: Optical discs always have greater capacity than HDDs
ROM is a USB storage device
SSD usually has faster access and greater shock resistance than HDD
An HDD contains no moving parts
quiz.why: SSD avoids spinning platters and read/write heads.
